idiom_name: protocol Mediator: AnyObject + weak var mediator + delegate/closure colleagues
implementation_notes: Swift's form is a protocol plus reference semantics: declare a protocol the hub conforms to (usually one notify/mediate method), give colleagues a weak var mediator so the hub does not keep them and they do not create a cycle, and let participants report events through it instead of holding each other. Protocols - with protocol extensions for shared behaviour - replace the abstract class, and closures or delegates replace concrete colleague references: the classic structure with ARC's ownership rules made explicit. Use it for view controllers, coordinators and small object graphs; when the need is app-wide broadcast, the NotificationCenter variant already provides the hub.
pitfalls: Colleagues must hold the mediator weakly and the mediator must not hold every colleague strongly, or the graph is a retain cycle that never deallocates - ARC leaks are silent.
Delegate protocols should be class-bound (AnyObject) so weak references compile; a value-type conformer would be copied and its notifications lost.
notify runs synchronously on the caller's thread, so UI updates from a background colleague must be dispatched to the main actor (MainActor/DispatchQueue.main).
Protocol witnesses mean dynamic dispatch; for a very hot hub a closure or a direct reference can be faster, so measure before optimising.

variants.name: Foundation NotificationCenter hub
variants.implementation_notes: Foundation supplies the hub: broadcasters post(name:object:userInfo:) and subscribers register with addObserver(forName:object:using:) (block-based, returning a token you must remove), or consume an async sequence via notifications(named:object:) - and Combine's publisher(for:object:) exposes the same notifications as a publisher. That replaces a hand-written mediator for cross-module broadcast (system events, app-wide state changes) because the observer registry, dispatch table and removal API are the framework's. Use a protocol mediator instead when the hub must implement coordination rules or return answers; NotificationCenter is one-way notification by design.
pitfalls: The block-based addObserver returns an opaque token; if it is not stored and passed to removeObserver, the block and everything it captures leaks and keeps firing - the classic observer leak.

Notifications are delivered synchronously on the posting thread by default, and the queue parameter applies only to the block-based API, so UI work still needs an explicit main-thread hop with the selector API.
Notification names are string-like and untyped, so a typo never fires and userInfo dictionaries push casts into observers; prefer the typed Message/AsyncMessage API or Combine publishers.
App-wide broadcast hides the collaboration graph, so overuse becomes action-at-a-distance with no compile-time contract.
